items.prompt: Priya's and Alex's zip files are both named "final". What is the core problem?
choices: Nothing in either file records which changes it contains or how it relates to the other
The zip format cannot hold source code files larger than a few megabytes
The filenames are too long to show both fixes at once
items.explanation: filenames are labels written by hand; they carry no recorded relationship between copies.

items.prompt: Which question can a zip file NOT answer by itself?
choices: What the file extension is
Why a change was made
How large the archive is
items.explanation: A zip holds contents only; the reason for a change lives in someone's head unless a message was recorded with it.

items.prompt: What does Git record at the moment of a commit that a manual copy does not?
choices: A bigger copy of the project saved to a second disk
A faster, compressed version of each of the files
A message explaining why, plus who and when
items.explanation: A commit carries metadata (author, time, message) alongside the snapshot.

items.prompt: Does Git record a checkpoint every time you press Save in your editor?
choices: No, only when you deliberately add and commit
Yes, every save in the editor automatically becomes a commit
Yes, but only when the editor is closed for the day
items.explanation: Saving changes the file on disk; a checkpoint exists only after git add and git commit.

items.prompt: Alex made his copy without opening Priya's. What is the missing piece?
choices: A faster internet connection to send the zip files
A recorded link showing which copy came from which
A larger hard drive to hold more copies of the zip
items.explanation: Without a recorded parent relationship nobody can tell whose work contains whose.

items.prompt: To find when a bug first appeared using only manual copies, you would have to:
choices: Run one command that lists every copy in order of date
Ask each zip file for its built-in history of changes
Open and test old copies one at a time
items.explanation: Manual copies have no ordered history, so each must be inspected by hand.

items.prompt: Why does renaming files more carefully (v2, v3, FINAL) not fix the problem?
choices: A better name is still just a label, not a recorded relationship
Names are limited to eight characters on most systems
Zip files ignore their names when they are opened
items.explanation: The gap is missing structure, and a more careful label does not add structure.

items.prompt: Which of these is a human-written substitute for a commit message?
choices: The file size shown in the folder listing
A note in a separate document explaining a change
The icon shown next to the file in the folder
items.explanation: Manual workflows keep reasons somewhere else, if anywhere; a commit message keeps them attached to the change.

items.prompt: Two teammates each hold a folder named project-final. Adding a README to each describing its contents is proposed as a fix. What is still unsolved?
choices: Nothing, the README fully replaces version history
Combining their edits safely, because nothing records the shared starting point
Nothing, because READMEs are checked automatically
Nothing, since a descriptive filename on each copy already records its origin and purpose
items.explanation: A README answers 'why' for one copy but does not record where each copy came from, so merging two copies still has no base to compare against.
items.reference:
Three questions a zip can't answer
1️⃣ Why did this change?
2️⃣ Which copy has both people's work?
3️⃣ When did the bug appear?
Why: all three need a recorded relationship between saved states, and a filename cannot hold one.
items.learnMore:
Copies versus history

A manual copy preserves content but loses context: who, why, and how it relates to the other copies. Version control adds that context at the moment of the change, so the questions become lookups instead of detective work.

Common mistake

Treating Git as automatic backups. Backups capture bytes; commits capture bytes, intent, and lineage.
items.reflection: A pile of copies with no recorded relationships is a problem outside software too: a shared document emailed back and forth, or a recipe tweaked by three relatives. What would you need recorded, at the moment of each change, to tell which version is the real one?

items.prompt: A bug is reported and you hold 40 dated zip files. Which is the real cost of manual copies here?
choices: The zips are too small to contain the bug
Zip files cannot be opened twice
Zip files are too large to open on an ordinary computer, so old copies get lost
No ordered, inspectable history, so locating the first bad copy means opening many by hand
items.explanation: Finding the arrival point needs ordered states you can step through; hand-kept copies give no guaranteed order or labels.

choices: Whether copies exist at all
Why each change was made
How big each copy is
Whether copies exist at all, since automatic saving cannot guarantee a copy was made

items.prompt: What does a commit store besides the snapshot itself?
choices: Only the filenames of the files that changed
Author, time, message, and a pointer to its parent
A full duplicate of the previous commit inside it
items.explanation: A commit is a snapshot plus metadata plus the parent link.

items.prompt: What is a commit's parent link?
choices: A link to the author's email, used to notify them
A link to the commit that will be made after it
A pointer to the commit that came directly before it
items.explanation: Each commit points backward, and the chain of those pointers is the history.

items.prompt: Can a commit be edited in place after it is made?
choices: No, commits are immutable
Yes, anytime by saving again
Yes, but only by the author's boss
items.explanation: Commits are immutable; 'changing' history creates new commits.

items.prompt: Does Git store a full snapshot or a list of edits per commit, conceptually?
choices: A list of line edits
A full snapshot of the project
Only the filenames that changed
items.explanation: Git's model is snapshots, with unchanged files shared by content.

items.prompt: A tracked file is one that:
choices: Has been deleted from the disk but not from Git
Is larger than 1 MB, so Git follows it specially
Git already knows belongs in history
items.explanation: Tracked means Git is already following it; untracked means visible but not yet promised.

items.prompt: An untracked file is:
choices: Visible to Git but not yet part of any commit
Permanently hidden from Git so it can never be added
Already committed twice on two different branches
items.explanation: Untracked files exist on disk but have never been added.

items.prompt: What does walking the parent links backward let you do?
choices: Delete the project and start over from the last zip
Return to any past state, not just the last one
Speed up your editor when it opens large files
items.explanation: Because every state is reachable via parents, any point in history can be inspected.

items.prompt: In the chain A, B, C (HEAD), which commit is the newest?
choices: A
B
C
items.explanation: HEAD marks where you are now; parents point back toward A.

items.prompt: Two commits have identical snapshots but different parents. Are they the same commit?
choices: Yes, only the snapshot matters
Yes, parents are optional decoration
No, the parent link and metadata are part of what identifies a commit
Yes, because two commits with the same files are always merged into one stored commit
items.explanation: A commit's identity includes its parent and metadata, so the same files in a different place in history are a different commit.
items.reference:
A commit, opened up
📸 the snapshot of the project
✍️ author, time, message
🔗 pointer to the parent commit
Why: the parent pointers are the history; without them you only have loose snapshots.
items.learnMore:
History is the links

A commit is not just saved files. The parent pointer turns separate snapshots into an ordered, walkable history, and immutability means that history can be trusted once written.

Common mistake

Thinking a commit is a list of edits. It represents a full snapshot; edits are computed by comparing two of them.
items.reflection: A chain where each entry points to the one before it is how a ledger, a family tree, or a chain of custody works. Where else does knowing exactly what came before something let you trust or reconstruct it?

items.prompt: Why can't you simply 'fix' an old commit's message in place?
choices: Commits are immutable, so a change creates a new commit with a new identity
Messages are stored on a server only
Git forbids typing in old commits
Git has no command to edit a message, so it can only be changed on the hosting server
items.explanation: Anything that identifies a commit is fixed; altering it means producing a different commit.

items.prompt: Which statement about the parent chain is most accurate?
choices: It only supports undoing the last action
It stores a diff you must replay forward
It is what lets you inspect or restore any past snapshot by walking backward
It exists only to display authorship, and plays no role in restoring older states
items.explanation: The chain gives access to every ancestor, which is stronger than single-step undo.

items.prompt: What is a branch?
choices: A full copy of the project saved in a new folder
A separate repository that lives only on a server
A movable label pointing at a commit
items.explanation: A branch is just a name that points at one commit.

items.prompt: Does creating a branch copy the project's files?
choices: No, it only adds a pointer
Yes, every file is duplicated
Yes, but only text files
items.explanation: Branch creation is instant because no files move.

items.prompt: What does 'distributed' mean for a Git clone?
choices: It holds only the newest versions of the files
It holds the entire history, not just the latest snapshot
It must stay online to read or write any history
items.explanation: Each clone is a complete copy of history.

items.prompt: Can you view history with no internet connection?
choices: No, history lives only on a server
Only for the last commit
Yes, the full history is local
items.explanation: A clone has everything needed to browse history offline.

items.prompt: Why can Git merge Priya's and Alex's work, when manual folders can't?
choices: Both lines remember the commit they started from
Git guesses which file is newer by its timestamp
Git picks the larger file and discards the other
items.explanation: The shared starting commit is the base for comparing each side's changes.

items.prompt: If the server disappears, what happens to a full clone?
choices: It becomes empty because history lived on the server
It still has the entire history
Only the latest commit survives in the clone
items.explanation: Distributed storage removes the single point of failure.

items.prompt: A merge commit is a snapshot that:
choices: Deletes a branch once its work is finished
Resets the project back to its very first state
Combines two lines of history
items.explanation: A merge has two parents, joining work that began from a common point.

items.prompt: Moving from branch 'main' to 'experiment' in a gitGraph picture means:
choices: Following a different label to a different commit
Copying the project into a new folder
Deleting main so only the new branch remains
items.explanation: Branches are labels; switching changes which one you are on.

items.prompt: Priya's login fix and Alex's tweak both started from commit B. After merging, why does the result have two parents?
choices: Git always creates two copies of the project
One parent is a backup
Because Git stores one extra backup copy of the project for each person who works on it
It joins two lines of history that diverged from a shared commit
items.explanation: A merge commit records both lines it combined, which manual folders cannot represent.
items.reference:
Branch and clone
🏷️ branch: a label on one commit, zero files copied
💻 clone: the complete history, on your machine
🔀 merge: joins two lines from a shared start
Why: cheap labels plus full local history is what makes safe experiments and offline work possible.
items.learnMore:
Why branching is cheap

History already exists as commits. A branch is only a name for one of them, so creating or deleting it never touches your files. Every clone repeats the same structure locally, which is why Git needs no central server to work.

Common mistake

Picturing a branch as a copied folder. It is a pointer to a commit.
items.reflection: Giving everyone a complete copy and a cheap way to try ideas on the side is a pattern with other uses: writers keeping drafts, or cooks testing a recipe change without touching the original. What would you try more freely if trying cost nothing and the original stayed safe?

items.prompt: A colleague says branching in Git must be slow for a huge repository. What is wrong with that claim?
choices: Branches are always compressed first
Creating a branch only writes a pointer, so cost does not grow with project size
Large repositories cannot have branches
Nothing is wrong, since larger repositories always need more files copied per branch
items.explanation: Because no files are copied, branch creation costs the same in a tiny and a huge project.

items.prompt: Conceptually, what does each Git commit represent?
choices: A full snapshot of the project
A diff against the previous commit
Only the files you named
items.explanation: Commits represent whole-project states.

items.prompt: Where do the diffs you see in git log -p come from?
choices: Stored line by line inside each commit as a list of edits
Computed on demand by comparing two snapshots
Typed in by the author when the commit is made
items.explanation: Diffs are derived for display, not the stored form.

items.prompt: If file X is unchanged between commits B and C, it is:
choices: Copied again in full into commit C
Deleted from B so that only C holds it
Stored once and referenced by both
items.explanation: Unchanged content is shared, not re-copied.

items.prompt: Why is committing fast even for large projects?
choices: Work scales with what changed, not total size
Git skips the work whenever a commit is large
Git compresses every file down to zero bytes
items.explanation: Only new content needs storing.

items.prompt: Which is closer to Git's model?
choices: A word processor's track-changes list of edits
A series of full pictures of the project
A single file that is edited in place over time
items.explanation: Snapshots, with sharing, rather than edit logs.

items.prompt: Does 'full snapshot' mean every commit physically copies every file?
choices: Yes, every file is copied in full every single time
Yes, though only for plain text files, not binaries
No, it describes what a commit represents, not what gets copied
items.explanation: Representation and physical storage differ.

items.prompt: Which command family displays differences between snapshots?
choices: git diff and git log -p
git branch
git init
items.explanation: Both compute differences from stored states.

items.prompt: Snapshot storage in Git is deduplicated by:
choices: Filename
Content
Author name
items.explanation: Identical content is stored once regardless of name.

items.prompt: A teammate says: 'git log -p proves Git stores diffs.' What is the best correction?
choices: The diff is computed at display time from two stored snapshots
git log -p stores a diff in a hidden file
Diffs are stored only for binary files
It proves nothing either way, since git log -p reads the diff from a hidden file in the commit
items.explanation: Display of a diff does not imply diffs are the stored form.
items.reference:
Stored versus shown
📸 Stored: snapshots (unchanged files shared)
🔍 Shown: diffs, computed on demand
Why: any two snapshots can be compared directly, so a diff never needs to be stored.
items.learnMore:
Snapshots, not diffs

Git's logical model is a series of complete project states. Sharing unchanged content keeps the physical cost low, and diffs are produced by comparing two states whenever you ask for one.

Common mistake

Assuming a commit is only the change. It is the whole state; the change is derived.
items.reflection: Photographs of a room at different times and a list of 'moved the lamp, painted the wall' describe the same changes in different forms. For which kinds of questions is each better, and what does storing full pictures make easy?

items.prompt: Commit C changes one line of one file in a 1,000-file project. What does C represent?
choices: Only the one changed line
A copy of all 1,000 files stored again
A complete project state, where 999 files are shared with earlier commits
A diff that must be replayed on top of the previous commit to rebuild the project
items.explanation: C is a full snapshot logically; physically only new content costs space.

items.prompt: Which design choice makes it cheap to compare commit B with commit Z, far apart in history?
choices: Both are whole snapshots, so Git compares them directly
Git replays every edit between B and Z
Git asks the author to summarize
Git must first convert both into diffs against the very first commit before comparing
items.explanation: With edit logs you replay a chain; with snapshots you compare two endpoints.

items.prompt: Which is the correct order of the three states?
choices: Repository, working directory, staging area
Working directory, staging area, repository
Staging area, repository, working directory
items.explanation: Files are edited, staged with git add, then committed.

items.prompt: What does git add do?
choices: Creates a permanent commit straight away
Deletes the file from disk and keeps a copy elsewhere
Copies the file's current content into the staging area
items.explanation: Add stages content for the next snapshot; it does not commit.

items.prompt: What does git commit record?
choices: What is currently staged
Everything on disk, including unstaged edits
Only new files that were never tracked before
items.explanation: A commit files exactly the staging area's contents.

items.prompt: In the desk/tray/archive picture, the staging area is the:
choices: The archive of the permanent record
Tray of pages about to be filed
The messy desk of files you are editing now
items.explanation: Staging is the in-between step before filing.

items.prompt: The working directory is:
choices: The permanent history of every commit
A list of the branches in the project
The files on disk right now
items.explanation: It is your current, editable copy.

items.prompt: You edited five files but staged three. A commit now includes:
choices: The three staged files
All five files
Only the two unstaged files
items.explanation: Unstaged changes stay in the working directory.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of the staging area?
choices: Making each of the files smaller on disk
Building a commit from some changes instead of all
Backing up every change to the cloud
items.explanation: It makes each commit a coherent, describable unit.

items.prompt: Which command shows what is staged versus not?
choices: git init
git clone
git status
items.explanation: Status reports each area's state.

items.prompt: You stage a file, then edit it again without re-staging, and commit. Which version is committed?
choices: The newest version on disk
The version staged earlier, not the newer edit
Both versions as two files
Neither, because commit refuses to run when a file is both staged and modified
items.explanation: Staging captures content at the moment of git add; later edits remain unstaged.
items.reference:
Three places, one flow
🖥️ Working directory: your messy desk
🧺 Staging area: the tray you are about to file
🗄️ Repository: the permanent archive
Why: git add moves content to the tray; git commit files only what is in the tray.
items.learnMore:
Staging is a deliberate snapshot

The staging area holds the content that was on disk when you ran git add. It does not track later edits, which is why the same file can be both 'staged' and 'modified' at once.

Common mistake

Assuming commit saves everything you changed. It saves only what you staged.
items.reflection: Sorting what goes into a letter before sealing the envelope is a small act of curation. Where else do you separate 'work in progress' from 'what I am ready to hand over', and what does that buffer protect you from?

items.prompt: A fix touches two unrelated concerns across five files. How does staging help?
choices: It merges the two concerns automatically
It hides the unrelated files forever
Staging merges the two concerns into one commit so the history stays short and tidy
Stage and commit each concern separately for two clear, describable commits
items.explanation: Selective staging splits one burst of editing into coherent commits.

The file is deleted

Branches are always created on a remote server
It only writes a new pointer to an existing commit

items.prompt: A branch points at:
choices: One commit
A whole folder
A list of files
items.explanation: A branch is a name for a commit.

items.prompt: After creating a branch, how many files were copied?
choices: All of them
None
Only the changed ones
items.explanation: Creation adds only a label.

items.prompt: Does branch creation cost more in a bigger project?

Yes, proportional to history length
No, the cost is the same

items.prompt: Which is the manual-copies equivalent of a branch?

Renaming a file and keeping the old name too
Deleting a folder once the work is done
items.explanation: Manual experiments mean full copies, and cost grows with size.

items.prompt: What adds actual content to a branch?
choices: Creating the branch itself, which adds only a label
New commits made on it
Switching to it, which only moves the current label
items.explanation: Only commits add content.

items.prompt: The sticky label analogy means a branch is like:
choices: A photocopy of the whole archive
A brand new archive built from scratch
A label on one page of the archive
items.explanation: Labels do not duplicate pages.

items.prompt: Two branches at the same commit share:
choices: Everything
Nothing
Only filenames
items.explanation: Same commit, same snapshot.

items.prompt: Branch creation takes 5 ms in a 5 KB project. Roughly how long in a 5 GB project?
choices: About a million times longer
Proportional to the number of files
About the same, since only a pointer is written
About a thousand times longer, since each of the files has to be copied into the new branch
items.explanation: A new ref file is tiny regardless of project size.

Branch cost
🏷️ Create: write one pointer (constant time)
📁 Manual copy: duplicate everything (grows with size)
➕ Only new commits add content
Why: a branch names an existing commit; nothing is duplicated.
items.learnMore:
A branch is a name, not a place

History is already stored as commits. A branch label picks one and moves forward as you commit, which is why making and deleting branches is effectively free.

Common mistake

Thinking each branch holds its own copy of the files.
items.reflection: A bookmark costs nothing, but marking your place lets you wander far and return. Where in your work does a nearly free 'mark this spot' let you take risks you would otherwise avoid?

items.prompt: After branching at commit C, you commit D on the branch and E on main. What do the two lines share?
choices: Commits up to C; D and E are separate
Nothing
Only E
Everything, including D and E, since branches always share every commit in a repository
items.explanation: History up to C is shared, later commits diverge.

items.prompt: What identifies a stored Git object?
choices: A hash of its content
Its filename in the directory
Its creation time on the disk
items.explanation: Content-addressing keys objects by their bytes.

items.prompt: Two identical files in different folders are stored:
choices: Twice
Once
Once per branch
items.explanation: Same bytes, same hash, one object.

items.prompt: If one byte of a file changes, its hash:
choices: Stays the same
Becomes zero
Changes
items.explanation: Different bytes give a different fingerprint.

items.prompt: Which hash function did this unit name for Git objects?
choices: SHA-1
MD5 only
CRC alone
items.explanation: Git objects were described as SHA-1 hashed.

items.prompt: Does the filename affect the content hash of a blob?
choices: Yes
No
Only on Windows
items.explanation: Only the bytes go into the blob hash.

items.prompt: Ten manual saves with one unchanged file store it:
choices: Once
Zero times
Ten times
items.explanation: Each zip holds its own copy.

items.prompt: Ten Git commits over one unchanged file store it:
choices: Once
Ten times
Five times
items.explanation: Each commit references the one stored object.

items.prompt: Content-addressing most directly explains why:
choices: Branches are given readable names
Snapshots are cheap even though they are full
Commits are given descriptive messages
items.explanation: Dedup by content keeps storage proportional to change.

items.prompt: A config file is re-added independently on two unrelated branches with identical bytes. How many stored objects result?
choices: Two, one per branch
Three, including the merge
Zero, since Git refuses to store a file whose content already appears anywhere in another branch
One, because the hash depends only on the bytes
items.explanation: Dedup is by content across the whole repository, not by adjacent commits.
items.reference:
Key = content
🔑 same bytes → same hash → stored once
✏️ one changed byte → new hash → new object
🚫 names and times are not part of the key
Why: storage cost follows distinct content, not number of commits.
items.learnMore:
Why dedup works

The hash is a pure function of content, so identical content collides on purpose, anywhere in the repository, and different content does not for practical purposes.

Common mistake

Believing Git compares only with the previous commit.
items.reflection: Identifying something by what it is, not what it is called, shows up in fingerprints, ISBNs, and checksums on downloads. Where else would knowing 'this is exactly the same thing' by its content alone save you from keeping duplicates?

items.prompt: A teammate says Git compares each new file to the previous commit's version to decide whether to store it. What is more accurate?
choices: Git diffs against the parent and stores the diff
Git hashes the content and checks whether that object already exists anywhere
Git always stores a new copy
Git compares file modification times and stores a file only when it is newer
items.explanation: The question asked is 'have I ever seen these exact bytes', not 'what changed from last time'.

Half of it
Several, since renaming changes the bytes of the file and so changes its stored hash
None, the same content object is referenced under a new name
items.explanation: Names live in directory listings; the content hash is unchanged.

items.prompt: What is hashed to produce a blob's ID?
choices: Only the filename and its folder
A header with the byte length, then the content
The author and the date it was saved
items.explanation: The blob header plus content go into SHA-1.

items.prompt: The blob header begins with which word?
choices: file
commit
blob
items.explanation: Blob objects are prefixed with the word blob.

items.prompt: What does the header contain after the word?
choices: The content's length in bytes
The filename and its extension
The branch name it was committed on
items.explanation: Length in bytes is part of the header.

items.prompt: Does the file's timestamp change its blob hash?
choices: Yes
No
Only if newer
items.explanation: Timestamps are not in the recipe.

items.prompt: Does the branch a file is on change its blob hash?
choices: Yes
Sometimes
No
items.explanation: Only bytes matter.

items.prompt: Which command prints a file's blob hash?
choices: git hash-object
git branch
git remote
items.explanation: hash-object reports the object ID for content.

items.prompt: The hash is therefore a pure function of:
choices: The editor used
The bytes
The time of day
items.explanation: Same inputs always give the same output.

items.prompt: The text 'hello' plus a newline is how many bytes?
items.explanation: Five letters plus one newline.

items.prompt: Two files look identical on screen, but one uses Windows line endings. What happens?
choices: They get different hashes because their bytes differ
They share one hash
Git refuses to store the second
They share one hash, because Git normalizes line endings automatically before every hash is made
items.explanation: Line endings are real bytes, so the content is different.
items.reference:
The blob hash recipe
📝 header: the word blob, a space, the byte length, a zero byte
📦 then the content bytes
🔢 SHA-1 of the whole thing is the object ID
Why: only bytes go in, so only bytes can change the ID.
items.learnMore:
Bytes, not appearance

Because the recipe sees only the header and bytes, 'hello' with a Unix newline and with a Windows newline are different objects. This is the reason line-ending normalization exists in Git.

Common mistake

Assuming that text which looks the same is the same content.
items.reflection: A fingerprint that depends only on content makes tampering and accidental differences visible. Where do you already trust a checksum or signature, and what invisible differences might it be catching for you?

items.prompt: A file's content is unchanged but its modified time is touched. What happens to its blob hash?
choices: It changes
It becomes invalid
It stays the same
It changes, because the modified time is recorded inside the blob header
items.explanation: Time is not an input, so the hash is stable.

choices: Compare byte lengths or hashes to find an invisible difference
Delete both and retype
Reinstall Git
Run git gc, which merges objects that merely look similar into a single stored object
items.explanation: Invisible byte differences, like carriage returns, explain most such cases.

items.prompt: A manual-copy strategy stores, for N saves of a project of size S:
choices: S
S divided by N
N times S
items.explanation: Every save is a full copy.

items.prompt: For Git, the first commit stores:
choices: The full project once
Nothing at all, since the first commit is empty
Half the project, to save space on the first commit
items.explanation: The first snapshot has nothing to share.

items.prompt: For later commits, Git stores mostly:
choices: The full project again
The changed portion
Only filenames
items.explanation: Unchanged content is referenced.

items.prompt: 20 manual saves of a 500 KB project total:
choices: 500 KB
975 KB
items.explanation: 20 times 500.

items.prompt: 20 Git commits of 500 KB with 5% changed total about:
choices: 975 KB
500 KB
items.explanation: 500 plus 19 times 25.

items.prompt: The more of the project changes per commit, the Git advantage:
choices: Grows
Shrinks
Stays the same
items.explanation: The savings are proportional to how little changes.

items.prompt: If 100% changes every commit, Git storage grows like:
choices: A flat line
Half of manual copies
Manual copies
items.explanation: Nothing is shared, so there is no saving.

items.prompt: Which workload gives Git the biggest advantage?
choices: Many commits with tiny changes
Few commits with total rewrites
One commit only
items.explanation: Dedup helps most when little changes.

items.prompt: A 200 KB project, 11 commits, 10% changed each time. About how much does Git store?
choices: 400 KB
220 KB
40 KB, since only the changed slice of the project is stored for the whole history
items.explanation: 200 plus 10 times 200 times 0.10 equals 400 KB.
items.reference:
Storage after 20 commits (500 KB)
🔴 Manual copies: 10,000 KB
🟢 Git, 5% changed: 975 KB
🟡 Git, 100% changed: 10,000 KB
Why: Git pays for what changes, so total rewrites erase the advantage.
items.learnMore:
Reading the formula

Git ≈ S + (N − 1) × S × f, with f the changed fraction; manual = N × S. As f approaches 1 the two converge. Binaries that change wholesale push f toward 1.

Common mistake

Treating the overall percentage as the whole story when a single large file changes completely.
items.reflection: A saving that depends on how little changes is a real but conditional benefit. Where else does a tool's advantage vanish when your workload stops matching its assumption, and how would you notice early?

items.prompt: A 400 KB video inside a 500 KB project is re-exported and committed whole each time. Why does one flat percentage mislead?
choices: Videos are free to store
Git compresses video to nothing
Videos make a project too large for Git to accept at all, regardless of how often they change
That one file behaves like 100% change, so overall growth is closer to manual copies
items.explanation: A binary that changes entirely each time has no shared content to dedup.

choices: Both double exactly
Manual doubles; Git grows by a much smaller step each time
Neither changes
Git doubles and manual copies stay flat, because zip files are compressed
items.explanation: Manual cost is linear in saves, Git's added cost per commit is only the changed slice.

items.prompt: What is the safest habit before each commit?
choices: Run git status to see what is staged
Delete every untracked file first
Commit twice in a row to be safe
items.explanation: Status shows exactly what will and won't be included.

items.prompt: A file you edited but never added is:
choices: Included automatically, since Git sees the edit
Left out of the commit
Deleted
items.explanation: Commit records only staged content.

items.prompt: Uncommitted work is part of permanent history:
choices: Yes
Only if staged
No
items.explanation: History starts at the commit.

items.prompt: Why commit early and often?
choices: The safety net starts at the first commit
Commits make every file smaller on disk
Git requires a commit every hour or it stops
items.explanation: Uncommitted work is hard to recover.

items.prompt: What file keeps node_modules out of Git?
choices: README.md
.gitignore
package.json
items.explanation: Ignore rules are set deliberately in .gitignore.

items.prompt: Should a .env with real secrets be committed?
choices: Yes
Only on main
No
items.explanation: Stored content stays in history permanently.

items.prompt: How can you get one file back as it was in an older commit?
choices: Restoring it from that past snapshot
Retyping it from memory as best you can
Emailing the file to a teammate to compare
items.explanation: Past states are addressable.

items.prompt: Large changing binaries in Git cause:
choices: Smaller repositories, since binaries compress well
Fast repository growth
No effect at all on repository size
items.explanation: Each change stores a new full blob.

items.prompt: You run git commit and your edited helper.js is missing from it. What most likely happened?
choices: Git ignores JavaScript
The commit was too large
It was never staged with git add
helper.js was committed to a different branch automatically, behind your back
items.explanation: Unstaged changes are skipped silently.
items.reference:
Where work is safe
🖥️ Working directory: not safe
🧺 Staging area: not safe
🗄️ Committed history: recoverable
Why: the safety net starts at the first commit.
items.learnMore:
Failure modes to remember

Forgotten git add, committed junk or secrets, trusting uncommitted work, and large changing binaries. Each has a simple preventive habit: check status, set .gitignore, commit early, keep media out of history.

Common mistake

Assuming a later delete cleans history. The old snapshot still contains it.
items.reflection: A safety net that only exists after you act raises the question of when to act. Where in your own work is 'save a checkpoint now, tidy later' the better habit, and what has losing something unsaved taught you?

items.prompt: Someone committed a build output folder and deletes it in the next commit. Is the repository size back to normal?
choices: No, the earlier commit still holds those objects in history
Yes, deletion removes them everywhere
Yes, after one hour
Yes, but only after running git status once, which cleans up the object store
items.explanation: Content-addressing keeps old snapshots intact, so history keeps the bytes.

Discarding changes that were never staged or committed
